cues.text: Bishop of Benevento
The Catholic Encyclopedia states plainly that 'with regard to the history of his life and martyrdom, we know next to nothing' about Januarius .
Beyond this, it identifies him as bishop of Benevento in southern Italy and records his martyrdom during the persecution of Diocletian around 305.
The surviving Acts of his life, though numerous, are all late compositions of uncertain historical worth.
Visiting the Imprisoned

Tradition relates that Januarius traveled to Pozzuoli to visit and encourage Christian deacons and laymen already imprisoned there for the faith, only to be arrested himself for his solidarity with them.
The ancient Roman Martyrology records that he was held with his own deacon, Festus, his lector, Desiderius, and several companions from neighboring towns.
Condemned to the Beasts
According to the traditional account, the group was first condemned to be thrown to wild bears in the amphitheater at Pozzuoli, but the animals inexplicably would not attack them.
The frustrated official in charge, attributing their survival to sorcery rather than divine protection, ordered the entire company beheaded instead.
The Blood Relic

Devout tradition holds that a woman named Eusebia gathered some of Januarius's blood after his execution and preserved it in glass vials, which were eventually enshrined alongside his body in Naples Cathedral .
Since at least the fourteenth century, this dried, solid mass has been reported to liquefy on set occasions each year.
This has been reported most notably on his September feast day, a phenomenon witnessed by enormous crowds and studied without a fully agreed natural explanation ever being established.
Patron Against Vesuvius
Januarius's relics have long been credited by the people of Naples with protecting the city from the eruptions of nearby Mount Vesuvius .
He remains the principal patron of the Archdiocese of Naples, his name inseparable from the city's civic and religious identity for over a thousand years.
Legacy

Whatever judgment history renders on the details of his martyrdom or the precise nature of the liquefaction associated with his relics, Januarius remains one of the most vividly and continuously venerated martyr-saints in the Catholic world.
His September feast still draws thousands to Naples Cathedral to witness the phenomenon that has borne his name popularly across the centuries: San Gennaro.
